title: Hello, Click: one value's round trip through a command line
premise: A caller has a Python function, `hello(count, name)`, and wants it to behave like a real command line program: `--count=3` typed on the command line, a name asked for interactively, output captured so a test can assert on it. Nothing in the function knows about argv, prompts, encodings, or exit codes. The data that arrives — the argument list `['--count=3']` and the keystrokes `'Click\n'` — has to cross from an untrusted outside world into a typed Python call, and a result has to come back out with an exit code that means something. This is the story of that crossing, and of the guarantees Click makes along the way.

chapters.title: Before the data: declarations become objects
chapters.data_in: the undecorated function `hello` plus decorator keywords: `default=1, help="Number of greetings."` and `prompt="Your name", help="The person to greet."`
chapters.data_out: `<Command hello>` carrying `params=[<Option count>, <Option name>]`, each with a resolved name, type and default
facts: `option()` builds an `Option` immediately and stashes it on `f.__click_params__`; `command()` pops that list, reverses it, and hands it to `Command(name='hello', callback=hello, params=[...])`, so declaration order in the source is the order in `Command.params`.

`--name` has no explicit `default`, so `Parameter.__init__` stores the sentinel `UNSET` and records `_default_explicit = False`. The sentinel is how Click later distinguishes "the user never supplied a default" from "the default is None".

Type is inferred, not required: `convert_type(None, UNSET)` falls through `_guess_type` to `STRING` for `--name`; the collapsed `--count` declaration passes `default=1`, so `_guess_type` returns `int` and the type becomes `INT`.
`_infer_flag_kind(is_flag=None, flag_value=UNSET)` returns `(False, False)` for `--name`: no flag_value, no secondary opts, `prompt_required` left at True, so it is an ordinary value option.

`_parse_decls` derives the Python name from the longest declaration: `'--name'` becomes `name`. `_check_name_is_usable` warns (DeprecationWarning, not an error) if that name is a Python keyword or not an identifier — a name that will become a `TypeError` in Click 9.0.
`_validate` runs only under `__debug__`; running Python with `-O` silences the illegal-combination checks (`nargs=-1` on an option, secondary flags on a non-boolean, `count` with `multiple`).

open_questions.question: `--name` ended up with a STRING type, no default, and a prompt string. Who turns that into an actual value, and what happens if nobody types anything?
`--count` was declared with `default=1` and type INT, but the command line will hand over the characters `'3'`. Where does the string become an integer, and what if it can't?

chapters.title: An isolated world: the runner swaps the process out from under you
chapters.data_out: three byte buffers `(stdout, stderr, output)` and a process whose `sys.stdin/stdout/stderr`, `termui` prompt hooks, `should_strip_ansi`, `pdb.Pdb.__init__` and `FORCED_WIDTH` have all been replaced
facts: `make_input_stream` turns `'Click\n'` into a `BytesIO`; `sys.stdin` becomes a `_NamedTextIOWrapper` over it, so the command's prompt reads from the test's string rather than a terminal.

`StreamMixer` gives stdout and stderr their own `BytesIOCopy`, each mirroring every write into a third shared buffer. That third buffer is what `Result.output` exposes, so interleaving reflects actual write order, not a post-hoc concatenation.

Default `capture='sys'` captures Python-level writes only. `_NamedTextIOWrapper.fileno()` keeps raising `io.UnsupportedOperation` (its `_original_fd` stays `-1`), which deliberately prevents user code doing `os.dup2(sys.stdout.fileno(), ...)` from clobbering the host test runner's stdout. `capture='fd'` opts into real fd redirection and is rejected on Windows.

Everything swapped is process-global: `sys.std*`, `os.environ` keys, `termui.visible_prompt_func`, `_compat.should_strip_ansi`, `pdb.Pdb.__init__`. The class docstring states this only works single-threaded; parallelism must be by process.
Environment overrides are recorded into `old_env` before mutation and restored in a `finally`, including deleting keys that were absent before.

`pdb.Pdb.__init__` is patched so a `breakpoint()` inside the command talks to `sys.__stdin__/__stdout__` (the real terminal) instead of the capture buffers. Debuggers that do not subclass `pdb.Pdb` are not covered.

open_questions.question: All of this global state is swapped before the command runs. If the command raises — or calls `sys.exit` — does the process get its streams, env and prompt hooks back?
Three buffers were created. What guarantees the mixed `output` buffer shows things in the order a user at a terminal would have seen them?

chapters.title: main(): the policy at the door
chapters.data_out: an untouched arg list, a completion check that found nothing, and control handed to `make_context` inside a layered `try`
facts: `args` was given explicitly, so `sys.argv[1:]` is not read and Windows glob/env expansion (`_expand_args`) is skipped; that expansion only happens when `args is None` and `os.name == 'nt'`.

Before any parsing, `_main_shell_completion` reads the environment variable `_HELLO_COMPLETE` (derived from `prog_name`, with `-` and `.` mapped to `_`). If that variable is set, Click runs the completion machinery and calls `sys.exit` — the program never reaches its own logic. This is a real trust boundary: an attacker-controlled environment can divert the invocation.

`standalone_mode=True` (the default) is the contract that `main` never returns normally: every path ends in `sys.exit`. With `standalone_mode=False`, exceptions propagate to the caller and the invoke return value comes back instead.

Each handler in the ladder does the same two things: re-raise when not standalone, otherwise set `report` (a callable that writes the message) and `exit_code`; the writing and exiting happen once, after the `try`.

`exit_code` is initialised to `1`, so any path that sets a message but no code reports failure. An `OSError` with `errno == EPIPE` is swallowed by wrapping `sys.stdout/stderr` in `_PacifyFlushWrapper`; any other `OSError` is re-raised.

open_questions.question: If the command succeeds, what exit code does the caller see, and who raises the `SystemExit` that produces it?
`--count=3` happens to be valid. Had it been `--count=x`, which handler would have caught it and what would the user have seen?

chapters.title: A context to live in
chapters.data_out: a `Context` with empty `params`, empty `args`, `help_option_names=['--help']`, a fresh `ExitStack`, pushed onto the thread-local stack with `_depth == 2`
facts: `make_context` merges `self.context_settings` into the keyword arguments only for keys the caller did not already pass, so explicit arguments to `main`/`invoke` win over command-level settings.

With no parent, defaults are taken from the command and from hard-coded values: `allow_extra_args = Command.allow_extra_args` (False), `allow_interspersed_args` True, `ignore_unknown_options` False, `help_option_names = ['--help']`, `resilient_parsing` False.
`auto_envvar_prefix` is `None` here, so no implicit environment variable lookup is enabled for any option. Automatic env reading only turns on when the caller opts in by passing a prefix.

`Context.scope(cleanup=False)` bumps `_depth` before entering, so the matching `__exit__` cannot run the close callbacks: resources opened during parsing (a `click.File` argument, say) stay open for the command body.
The context is pushed onto a `threading.local` stack; `get_current_context()` and therefore `pass_context`, `echo`'s colour default, and `resolve_color_default` all read from that stack.

open_questions.question: Parsing registers close callbacks on the context's ExitStack but is told not to clean up. When does anything actually get closed?

chapters.title: Building the parser, and the help option nobody declared
chapters.data_out: an `_OptionParser` with `--count`, `--name` and `--help` registered, and `Command.params` now holding a cached third option named `_click_default_help`
facts: `get_help_option_names` starts from `ctx.help_option_names` and removes any name already claimed by a user parameter, so declaring your own `-h/--help` silently suppresses the automatic one instead of colliding.

The automatic help option stores its value under the reserved name `_click_default_help`, which is why a user parameter literally named `help` no longer breaks parsing (`_HELP_OPTION_STORAGE_NAME`, core.py:61).
The help option object is cached in `Command._help_option` because `iter_params_for_processing` sorts by object identity; recreating it per call would break callback ordering.

`get_params` also runs the duplicate-name policing: a repeated option spelling, a user parameter squatting on the reserved help name, or an `Argument` sharing a storage name with another parameter each raise a `UserWarning`. All of this lives inside `if __debug__`, so under `python -O` the silent-overwrite footguns are not reported at all.

`Option.add_to_parser` translates declarative settings into parser actions: `store` here, `append` for `multiple`, `count` for counters, and `*_const` for flags with `const=self.flag_activation_value` — the resolver that turns an `UNSET` `flag_value` into `True` for boolean flags.

open_questions.question: A `--help` option now exists that the author never asked for, and its value will be computed on every run. Does it cost anything on a run that does not pass `--help`?

chapters.title: Tokens become a raw dict
chapters.data_out: `({'count': '3'}, [], [<Option count>])` — a raw string value, no leftovers, and the invocation order
facts: `--count=3` is split on the first `=`; the explicit value is pushed back onto `rargs` and consumed as the option's value, so values containing `=` survive intact.
The parser performs no type conversion and no validation: it yields the string `'3'`. Types are a higher layer entirely.
`state.order` records parameters in the order the user mentioned them. That list, not the declaration list, drives callback ordering later.

Roads not taken, all visible in this code: a bare `--` returns early and stops option parsing; an unknown long option raises `NoSuchOption` with `difflib` close matches unless `ignore_unknown_options` pushes it into leftovers; an option that needs a value but sees the next token starting with a prefix yields the `FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE` sentinel if `_flag_needs_value`, otherwise raises `BadOptionUsage`.
`parse_args` swallows `UsageError` entirely when `ctx.resilient_parsing` is set — the mode shell completion runs in. In normal operation it propagates.
With no positional parameters declared, `_unpack_args([], [])` returns `((), [])` and there are no leftover args.

chapters.title: Deciding who goes first
chapters.data_in: invocation order `[<Option count>]`, declaration order `[count, name, _click_default_help]`
facts: The sort key is `(not is_eager, index-in-invocation-order)`, with `float('inf')` for parameters the user never mentioned. Eager parameters therefore always run before non-eager ones, and within each group the user's command line order is respected.

Because `--help` (and `--version`, built the same way) is eager, its callback can print and exit before any other parameter is validated — that is the guarantee that `prog --help` works even when required options are missing.

`--name`, never mentioned on the command line, sorts last. Parameters that were absent still get processed, which is what makes a missing-value prompt or a default-from-another-parameter callback possible.

chapters.title: The help option that was never passed
chapters.data_in: `opts={'count': '3'}` and the help option, which appears nowhere in it
chapters.data_out: `(None, [])` — value `False`, source `DEFAULT`, callback invoked and did nothing, `ctx.params` untouched
facts: `consume_value` establishes a fixed precedence, most explicit first: command line, then environment variable, then `ctx.default_map`, then the parameter's own default. The resulting `ParameterSource` is recorded on the context and is queryable by user code via `ctx.get_parameter_source(name)`.
No envvar was declared and `auto_envvar_prefix` is None, so `resolve_envvar_value` returns None without reading `os.environ` at all.

The raw `default` is still the `UNSET` sentinel; `_resolve_lazy_default` turns it into `False` because this is a non-required boolean flag. Resolving lazily here (rather than in `__init__`) is what keeps `default is UNSET` a reliable answer to "did the author pass a default?".

The callback runs even though the user never passed `--help`: `show_help` receives `value=False` and returns immediately. The same shape guards `version_option`, which also returns early under `ctx.resilient_parsing` so completion never prints a version.
The result is discarded: `expose_value=False` means the winner of the slot arbitration does not write `ctx.params`, so the function signature never has to mention `_click_default_help`.

`handle_parse_result` arbitrates when several parameters share a storage name (feature switches): a more explicit source wins; on a tie, an explicitly-set default beats an auto-derived one; a loser's source is restored so later lookups stay truthful.

`augment_usage_errors` wraps the whole block, attaching `ctx` and `param` to any `BadParameter`/`UsageError` raised inside — that is how a type failure in a callback still reports which option caused it.
In `resilient_parsing` mode a conversion failure here is swallowed and the value reset to `UNSET`, so an invalid value cannot stop `--help` or shell completion from working.

answers.answer: The injected help option is evaluated on every run: envvar lookup, default resolution, a `BoolParamType` conversion of `False`, and a callback call that returns at once. The cost is a handful of calls and no observable effect, because `expose_value=False` keeps it out of `ctx.params`.

chapters.title: The caller's '3' and the user's 'Click'
facts: `--count` is found in `opts`, so its source is `COMMANDLINE` and `type_cast_value` runs `IntParamType` on `'3'`, producing `3`. Had the token been `'x'`, `_NumberParamTypeBase.convert` would have called `fail`, raising `BadParameter` — a `UsageError` subclass with `exit_code = 2`.

`--name` is absent from `opts`, has no envvar, no default map entry, and its default is still `UNSET`. Because `prompt` is set, `prompt_required` is True and `resilient_parsing` is False, `consume_value` calls `prompt_for_value` and records the source as `PROMPT`.

`prompt_for_value` computes the default *before* any interaction, then calls `termui.prompt` with `value_proc=lambda x: self.process_value(ctx, x)` — so the parameter's type and callback validate prompted input exactly as they validate command line input, and an invalid answer re-asks rather than crashing.

Under isolation, `termui.visible_prompt_func` is the runner's `visible_input`: it writes the prompt to the captured stdout, reads one line from the `BytesIO` stdin, echoes it back, and strips the newline. That is why the expected output begins with `Your name: Click`.

If stdin were exhausted, `visible_input` raises `EOFError`; `main`'s handler turns `EOFError`/`KeyboardInterrupt` into a blank line on stderr plus `Aborted!` and a non-zero exit. A prompting option therefore fails loudly, not silently, in a non-interactive pipeline.
Had `--name` had no prompt and no default, `process_value` would have raised `MissingParameter` instead; with `prompt` and `resilient_parsing` set (completion), the prompt is skipped entirely.

After all parameters are processed, `parse_args` sweeps `ctx.params` and rewrites any remaining `UNSET` to `None`, so the sentinel is never visible to user code. Leftover args would have triggered `ctx.fail('Got unexpected extra argument...')` here, because `allow_extra_args` is False for a plain `Command`.

answers.answer: `Option.consume_value` finds no value for `--name` from any source and, because `prompt` is set, calls `prompt_for_value`, which reads the line `Click` through the runner's patched prompt hook and marks the source `PROMPT`. With nothing to read, the prompt raises `EOFError` and the run aborts with a non-zero exit code.

`Parameter.type_cast_value` applies the inferred `IntParamType` to the parser's raw `'3'`, yielding `3`. A non-numeric token makes the type call `fail`, raising `BadParameter` — a `UsageError`, exit code 2, with the offending option named via `augment_usage_errors`.

chapters.title: Out of parsing, into the call
chapters.data_in: the context with `params={'count': 3, 'name': 'Click'}` and `_depth` unwinding to 0
chapters.data_out: the context re-entered by `main`, then by `ctx.invoke`, with the callback about to be called as `hello(count=3, name='Click')`
facts: The `scope(cleanup=False)` exit drops `_depth` from 2 to 1, so `_close_with_exception_info` is not called: nothing opened during parsing is closed yet. `main` then re-enters the same context with `with`, taking `_depth` back to 1 and arming a real teardown for later.
`Command.invoke` would echo a red `DeprecationWarning:` line to stderr first if the command were marked `deprecated`; it is not, so it goes straight to the callback.

`ctx.invoke(self.callback, **ctx.params)` splats the parameter dict as keyword arguments. That is the reason parameter names must be valid Python identifiers, and why a name like `from` is only reachable through `**kwargs`.
`augment_usage_errors(self)` wraps the callback call, so a `UsageError` raised inside user code still carries the context and prints usage.

When `invoke` is handed a `Command` rather than a plain callable, it builds a sub-context and fills every missing parameter from `get_default`, mapping `UNSET` to `None` because the sentinel is deliberately kept out of the public API.

answers.answer: Nothing closes at the end of parsing: `scope(cleanup=False)` keeps `_depth` above zero. The ExitStack is unwound later, by `ctx.exit()`/`Context.__exit__` once `main`'s `with` block finishes — after the command body has had its chance to use the resources.

chapters.title: echo, three times
chapters.data_in: the string `'Hello, Click!'`, emitted once per iteration of `range(3)`
chapters.data_out: `b'Hello, Click!\n'` written and flushed into the captured stdout buffer and mirrored into the mixed output buffer; the callback returns `None`
facts: With `file=None`, `echo` resolves the stream through a `WeakKeyDictionary`-backed cache keyed on the current `sys.stdout`, so the wrapper is built once per stream, and swapping `sys.stdout` (as the runner does) yields a different cache entry rather than a stale one.

`_force_correct_text_stream` returns the runner's UTF-8 wrapper unchanged because its `encoding`/`errors` are compatible and `_stream_is_misconfigured` is False. The rewrap path exists for the ASCII-encoding case, where Click deliberately forces UTF-8 with `errors='replace'` — mojibake instead of a crash.

Colour handling is a default with teeth: `color=None` consults `resolve_color_default`, which reads `ctx.color` (None here), and then `should_strip_ansi`. Normally that answers "strip unless `isatty()`", so piping output removes ANSI codes; here the runner's patched version answers True because `color=False` was requested.
`echo` always flushes, and routes `bytes`/`bytearray` to the underlying binary writer when one can be found, so writing bytes to a text stream works instead of raising.
`BytesIOCopy.write` writes to the shared mixed buffer *before* its own, and `flush` flushes both — that is the mechanism behind faithful stdout/stderr interleaving.
If no standard stream exists at all (pythonw on Windows), `echo` returns silently rather than raising.

answers.answer: Every write to the captured stdout or stderr goes through `BytesIOCopy.write`, which first appends the same bytes to the single shared `output` buffer. Ordering in `Result.output` is therefore the real write order across both streams, including the prompt echo that `visible_input` wrote before the three greetings.

chapters.title: Exit is an exception
chapters.data_out: `Exit(0)` raised, the ExitStack unwound with the exception info, caught by `main`, `sys.exit(0)`
facts: The return value of the command is deliberately *not* used as the exit code. The comment at core.py:1591-1597 spells out why: a callback returning `1`, or a chained group returning `[None, None]`, would make truthiness a misleading success signal. Success is always `ctx.exit()` with code 0.
`ctx.exit` closes the context *before* raising `Exit`, so `call_on_close` callbacks and `with_resource` context managers run even on an early exit (changed in 8.2).

`Context.__exit__` forwards the live exception type, value and traceback into `ExitStack.__exit__`, so a registered resource can observe and even suppress the failure; its return value becomes the `with` block's result. After unwinding, a fresh `ExitStack` is installed so the context can be reused.
`main` catches `Exit`, takes `e.exit_code` as the process exit code, leaves `report` unset, and falls through to `sys.exit(0)`.

The outermost `except (EOFError, KeyboardInterrupt)` wraps even the reporting step: if the user interrupts while the error message is being written, the message may be lost but the intended exit code still wins. That is a stated policy choice, not an oversight.

answers.answer: Exit code 0, raised by `sys.exit(exit_code)` at the end of `main` after `ctx.exit()` raised `Exit(0)` and the `except Exit` handler copied its code. The command's return value plays no part.

`--count=x` would raise `BadParameter` inside `handle_parse_result`; `main`'s `except ClickException` would set `report = e.show` and `exit_code = e.exit_code` (2 for a `UsageError`). `UsageError.show` prints the usage line, a `Try 'hello --help' for help.` hint built from the longest help name, then `Error: Invalid value for '--count': ...` to stderr.

chapters.title: What the caller gets back
chapters.data_in: the `SystemExit(0)` escaping `cli.main`, plus the three byte buffers
chapters.data_out: `Result(exit_code=0, exception=None, output_bytes=b'Your name: Click\nHello, Click!\n...')` and `result.output` as a `str`
facts: `SystemExit` is caught separately from other exceptions: a code of `None` becomes 0, a non-zero code is also stored as `result.exception`, and a non-integer code is written to stdout and coerced to 1. So `exit_code == 0` with `exception is None` is the success signal.

`catch_exceptions` defaults to True, which means a genuine bug in the command surfaces only as `exit_code == 1` plus `result.exception`/`exc_info`. A test that asserts only on `output` can pass while the command crashed — a real misuse hazard, mitigated by passing `catch_exceptions=False`.
The `finally` inside `invoke` flushes both streams and, in `fd` mode, stops the `_FDCapture`s and merges their bytes into the same buffers, so late or C-level writes are not lost.

`isolation`'s own `finally` restores `sys.std*`, `os.environ`, the `termui` prompt hooks, both `should_strip_ansi` references, `FORCED_WIDTH` and `pdb.Pdb.__init__` — unconditionally, whatever happened inside.
`_NamedTextIOWrapper.close` is a deliberate no-op: the buffer belongs to the `StreamMixer`, so the default `__del__` must not close it out from under the `Result`.
`Result.output` decodes with `errors='replace'` and normalises `\r\n` to `\n`, so undecodable bytes never raise when a test reads the output.

answers.answer: Yes. Both teardown paths are `finally` blocks: `invoke`'s flushes and merges the captured bytes, and `isolation`'s restores every piece of swapped global state — streams, environment keys, prompt hooks, `should_strip_ansi`, forced width and the pdb patch — regardless of whether the command returned, exited, or raised.
